issues.legal_issue: A contractual claim for monetary relief against a state instrumentality may be pursued through writ jurisdiction when the instrumentality’s conduct is arbitrary and the claim does not require resolution of disputed facts.
material_facts: The claim arose from a development agreement with a state instrumentality, which had received the developer’s payments but did not convey the promised land or refund the principal.
The instrumentality did not dispute the developer’s entitlement to a refund or the unavailability of the land for the project.
The agreement contained an arbitration clause, but the basic facts relevant to the refund claim were not in dispute.
issues.conclusion: The writ petition was maintainable. Contractual subject matter and an arbitration clause did not, by themselves, exclude writ jurisdiction in these circumstances.
issues.legal_principle: Article 226 permits enforcement of contractual rights against the State or its instrumentalities in an appropriate case, including a claim for monetary relief. The court must exercise that jurisdiction with circumspection, particularly where disputed facts require a trial; however, an alternative contractual remedy does not bar relief where state action is arbitrary or unreasonable and violates Article 14. The Court relied on ABL International Ltd. v. Export Credit Guarantee Corporation of India, including its discussion of Whirlpool Corporation v. Registrar of Trade Marks; State of U.P. v. Sudhir Kumar; Popatrao Vynkatrao Patil v. State of Maharashtra; and Harbanslal Sahnia v. Indian Oil Corporation and Ram Barai Singh & Co. v. State of Bihar.

rule.if: contractual_writ_proceeding and state_instrumentality_acted_arbitrarily and (foundational_representation_failed or material_facts_undisputed)

predicates.contractual_writ_proceeding: A claimant seeks contractual relief through a writ proceeding against the State or one of its instrumentalities.
predicates.state_instrumentality_acted_arbitrarily: The state instrumentality acted unfairly or unreasonably in dealing with the claimant.
predicates.foundational_representation_failed: A representation fundamental to the parties’ contract proved false or could not be fulfilled.
predicates.material_facts_undisputed: The material facts necessary to decide the claim are not disputed and do not require an evidentiary trial.

issues.definition: When a claimant seeks contractual relief by writ against a state instrumentality, arbitrary conduct together with a failed foundational representation or undisputed material facts supports the availability of the writ remedy.

issues.legal_issue: A developer is entitled to recover payments made under a public project contract when the state entity’s promised title fails and the land consequently cannot be used for the project.
material_facts: The developer paid the purchase price, earnest money and project development expenses required under the project documents.
The development agreement represented that the state entity could transfer the project land with title free from encumbrances and required it to execute a sale deed after payment.
The land dispute ultimately resulted in a final determination that the government did not have title to the project land, and the project could not proceed on that land.
The agreement provided for compensatory payment if the state entity could not execute the sale deed or a political force majeure event materially affected the project.
issues.conclusion: The developer was entitled to a refund of the amounts paid together with contractual compensatory interest.
issues.legal_principle: The development agreement’s Articles 3.1, 14.3.1 and 17.6, read with its definitions of compensatory payment and applicable rate, provided for repayment with interest where the promised transfer could not be completed or a qualifying political force majeure event affected the project. The failure of the title on which the contract was founded entitled the developer to enforce that remedy. The State and its instrumentalities remain bound by Article 14 of the Constitution to act fairly in contractual dealings and must make good representations on which private parties invest. The Court relied on State of Andhra Pradesh through Principal Secretary v. Pratap Karan; ABL International Ltd. v. Export Credit Guarantee Corporation of India; Indsil Hydropower v. State of Kerala; and Central Bank of India v. Devi Ispat Ltd.

rule.if: contractual_refund_claim and developer_paid_required_consideration and state_entity_failed_to_convey_promised_title and title_failure_made_project_unavailable

predicates.contractual_refund_claim: A developer seeks repayment under a contract for a public project.
predicates.developer_paid_required_consideration: The developer paid the consideration required by the project contract.
predicates.state_entity_failed_to_convey_promised_t: The state entity did not convey the title it had undertaken to transfer.
predicates.title_failure_made_project_unavailable: The failure of title meant that the land could not be used for the contracted project.

issues.definition: A developer who paid the required consideration under a public project contract is entitled to repayment with contractual interest when the state entity fails to convey promised title and that failure makes the project land unavailable.

issues.legal_issue: Contractually defined compensatory interest accrues from the dates on which the developer made the respective payments, rather than only from the date on which the developer later demanded a refund.
material_facts: The development agreement defined compensatory payment to include interest on the purchase price from the date the first payment was made.
The developer made payments in instalments under the project documents.
The developer’s later awareness of the pending title litigation and its decision to continue pursuing the project did not change the contractual commencement date for compensatory payment.
issues.conclusion: Interest was payable from the respective dates on which the payments were made; limiting interest to the later refund demand was an error.
issues.legal_principle: The express terms of the development agreement governed the commencement of compensatory interest. The agreement provided for interest from the date of the first payment of the purchase price; the Court applied that provision to the respective payments and held that the developer’s effort to continue with the project did not forfeit that contractual entitlement. The Court relied on the compensatory-payment definition in Article 1 and Article 14.3.1 of the development agreement.

predicates.contractual_compensatory_interest_claim: A developer seeks compensatory interest under a project contract.
predicates.agreement_sets_interest_start_at_payment: The contract specifies that compensatory interest begins when payment is made.
predicates.developer_made_payments_before_refund_de: The developer made the relevant payments before later requesting a refund.

issues.definition: Where a developer claims contractual compensatory interest and the contract starts interest at payment, interest accrues from the payment dates even if the refund is demanded later.

issues.legal_issue: A contractually specified annual-compounding interest rate may be reduced to non-compounded interest when compounding is unconscionable in the circumstances.
material_facts: The agreement specified interest at the State Bank of India prime lending rate compounded annually.
The developer knew of the pending litigation over title when it entered the development agreement and continued to pursue the project while the dispute remained unresolved.
The Court nevertheless allowed the contractual rate of interest but declined to allow compounding.
issues.conclusion: Interest was payable at the contractual rate without annual compounding.
issues.legal_principle: Under Central Bank of India v. Ravindra, a court may reduce a stipulated interest rate that is penal, excessive or part of a substantially unfair transaction. Section 74 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 permits a court to reduce contractually stipulated interest that is penal, excessive or in terrorem. The Court relied on K. P. Subbarama Sastri v. K. S. Raghavan, Oriental Kuries Ltd. v. Lissa and Bhubaneshwar Development Authority v. Susanta Kumar Mishra. Considering the developer’s knowledge of the pending title litigation and its decision to continue with the project, the Court found compounding unconscionable while allowing interest at the contractual rate.

rule.if: contractual_compounding_claim and claimant_knew_title_litigation and claimant_chose_to_continue_project and interest_would_compound_annually

predicates.contractual_compounding_claim: A claimant seeks interest compounded under the terms of a contract.
predicates.claimant_knew_title_litigation: The claimant knew that litigation concerning the relevant title was pending when it entered the contract.
predicates.claimant_chose_to_continue_project: The claimant continued to pursue the project while the title dispute remained unresolved.
predicates.interest_would_compound_annually: The contractual interest term would compound interest annually.

issues.definition: When a claimant seeks annual compounding despite knowing of a title dispute and choosing to continue the project, the court may award the contractual interest without compounding.

issues.legal_issue: A successor state instrumentality directed to make a refund must pay the claimant without that payment awaiting final resolution of an inter-instrumentality apportionment dispute.
material_facts: The project contract and the relevant land transaction originated with a corporation of the former state, and the land was situated in the territory of a successor state.
The successor-state corporation disputed whether the refund liability should be shared with the predecessor corporation under the reorganisation arrangements.
The record included a demerger scheme and a certificate stating that assets and liabilities had been apportioned; the project area fell within the successor-state corporation’s operational region.
The Court left the merits of the competing corporations’ apportionment claims undecided.
issues.conclusion: The successor-state corporation was required to pay the amounts due to the developer, while remaining free to pursue an apportionment claim against the other corporation in accordance with law.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 68 and 53 of the Andhra Pradesh Reorganisation Act, 2014 address apportionment of the assets, rights and liabilities of specified corporations; Sections 65 and 66 provide for agreed apportionment and certain adjustments; Section 71 permits directions concerning interests and shares in specified companies. Applying that scheme to the record, the Court did not finally decide the corporations’ rights inter se. It required the successor-state corporation to pay the claimant and preserved its right to pursue apportionment in accordance with law.

predicates.refund_appeal_with_intercorporate_alloca: A refund claim is before the court and successor entities dispute how the liability is allocated between them.
predicates.successor_entity_is_responsible_for_the_: The project area falls within the operational region assigned to a successor entity under the relevant reorganisation arrangements.
predicates.successor_entity_contests_allocation_of_: A successor entity disputes whether it must bear the whole liability or may seek to share it with another entity.

issues.definition: In a refund appeal involving disputed allocation between successor entities, the entity responsible for the project area must pay the claimant while its inter-entity allocation claim remains open.

issues.legal_issue: Non-payment of stamp duty or lack of registration does not, by itself, defeat a claim for compensatory payment under a development agreement.
material_facts: The developer relied on a development agreement that had not been registered or assessed to stamp duty.
The agreement placed responsibility for stamp duty and registration fees on the developer.

The Court directed that the agreement be impounded and sent for stamp-duty assessment and registration formalities, with the refunding entity to pay the determined charges initially and deduct them from the refund.
issues.conclusion: The claim could not be defeated solely because stamp duty had not been paid; the agreement had to be impounded and processed for assessment and registration, with the charges handled as directed.
issues.legal_principle: The Stamp Act is a fiscal measure intended to secure state revenue, not a technical weapon for an opposing party to defeat a claim. The Court relied on Hindustan Steel Limited v. Dilip Construction Company and directed impounding and assessment of the agreement, followed by registration formalities and payment of the determined charges.

predicates.contractual_compensation_claim: A claimant seeks compensatory payment under an agreement.
predicates.agreement_is_unstamped_or_unregistered: The agreement relied on for the claim has not been duly stamped or registered.
predicates.nonpayment_is_the_only_objection_to_the_: The asserted defect in stamp duty or registration is the sole basis advanced for defeating the claim.

issues.definition: When a claimant seeks contractual compensation and the only objection is that the agreement is unstamped or unregistered, the claim is not defeated on that ground and the agreement is processed for stamp and registration requirements.
